This system of pigment classification follows in general that of Schwartz (1957), except that the dursal heasey fleeking classification uses only four categories rather than five.
Table III gives a comparison of coloration of several escarpment populations of jurdani. As shown, the greatest degree of iridophore flecking and spotting occurs in the Joeassee and Burrells Mountain populations. Both of these areas are located at the homotory of the Blue Ridge near the edge of the contiguous range of jurdani. At Buck Knob, 1½ uniles to the northeast of Burrells Mountain, the juriani population shows a slight decrease in iridophore pigmentation, suggesting a clinal decrease in a south-to-north direction. This inference is reinforced by data from a small sample of jurdani collected two miles north of Buck Knob at the Sloan Bridge locality.
The jurilani sample from the Upper Falls in Whitewater Gorge shows a much lower percentage of iridophore piguientation than at Jocassee. To the northwest at Flat Mountain and Little Terrapin Mountain the decrease in dorsal flecking continues, although without much corresponding change in lateral spotting. In the Carniers sample the incidence of flecking and spotting is similar to that found in the rearby Whitewater samples: however, at Cashiers the distribution of iridophores is more limited than at other localities, as brassy flecks are largely confined to the head and eyelids, and white spots to the checks and shoulders.

This gradual cline may be sharper to the north and mortheast of Jogassee, since no evidence of iridoptore pignientation was found in the Toxaway populations of jordani in North Carolina. However, since no collecting was dene to the immediate north or mortheast of Jorassee in South Carolina, nothing is known of variation of jordani in this area. In Thompson Gorge, just east of Whitewater, two out of six specimens taken adjacent to the 2503-foot level of the river were lightly flecked with brassy. These meager data suggest a cline similar to that in Whitewater Gorge.
Gordon (1960) in the Highlands area observed brassy flecking only in small jordani under 50 mm, in shout-vent length. The present study found iridophores not confined to any age or size class in the incarpment popullations, although in some there is a trend toward reduced fleeking in older individuals. The two nearest localities to HighLunds, Little Terrapin Mountain and Cashiers, render comparisons: At the former, of 40 specimens under 50 mm., 15 showed brassy fleeking (37 per cent), while only 6 of 26 individuals over 50 mm, exhibited fleeking (23 per cent). At Cashiers 9 rat of 18 salamanders under 50 mm. showed brassy flecking (50 per cent). while 7 out of 22 specimens over 50 mm, were flecked (32 per cent).
Introgression Between Plethodon glutinosus and P. jordani
At one locality, Moody Spring, the Plethodon were difficult to allocate. This is the southernmost locality, lying near the homalary of the escarpment and Pirelmont.
Plethulon were scarce at Moody Spring: only 23 individuals were collected on six occasions. Several other collecting traps yielded no salamanders despate intensive scarcing; apparently the density of Plethulon is low in this area. Table II shows that these Plethulon attain a size similar to that of glutinosus. In pagmentation they are characterized by heavy white to yellow bleteining on the sides and throat; the blotches are as well developed as in any glutinosus or joudant from the escarganent.
